Wizard
WIZ-erd
noun
From Middle English wys, “wise,” with the suffix -ard: a “wise one.” But the wisdom the AV names is stolen and damnable — the wizard traffics with familiar spirits — and the modern hero-wizard of story has the word exactly upside down.

Biblical Definition

In the KJV a wizard is no white-bearded hero but a capital criminal. The word is simply a “wise one” — Middle English wys with a suffix — yet the wisdom it names is stolen and damnable: the wizard is a man who traffics with familiar spirits and gives out occult knowledge, and the modern reader who pictures Merlin or the kindly sorcerer of a children’s tale has the word exactly upside down. Scripture always pairs him with the medium and always under sentence. “Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them” (Lev 19:31) — to seek the wizard is to be defiled by him. The penalty is death: “A man also or woman that hath a familiar spirit, or that is a wizard, shall surely be put to death” (Lev 20:27). Manasseh’s wicked reign is summed up in the arts he revived — he “dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger” (2Ki 21:6). And Isaiah mocks the whole guild for the thin, ghostly noise it makes, calling men from “wizards that peep, and that mutter” (Isa 8:19) to seek instead the living God. The wizard’s wisdom is a whisper from the pit; the fear of the LORD is the beginning of the wisdom that is true.

Webster 1828 Definition

A man who practices the occult arts and traffics with familiar spirits — a male medium, not a hero of story.

WIZARD, a man who practices magic arts and pretends to occult knowledge; one that hath a familiar spirit.

From Middle English wys, “wise,” with the suffix -ard: a “wise one,” but wise in forbidden things.

Scripture pairs the wizard always with the medium and always under the death sentence.

To seek after wizards is to be defiled by them (Lev 19:31); the wizard shall surely be put to death (Lev 20:27).

Isaiah scorns the wizards that peep and mutter, when a people might seek their God (Isa 8:19).

Key Scripture

Lev 19:31 — "Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God."

Lev 20:27 — "A man also or woman that hath a familiar spirit, or that is a wizard, shall surely be put to death: they shall stone them with stones: their blood shall be upon them."

2Ki 21:6 — "And he made his son pass through the fire, and observed times, and used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger."

Isa 8:19 — "And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?"

Modern Corruption

The word has been turned inside out: the AV’s wizard is a condemned occultist, while the modern wizard is a beloved hero of fantasy — and beneath the story lies a real revival of male occult practice.

expand to see more

Here is a reversal worth naming plainly, for it shapes how a whole culture reads the word. In the AV a wizard is a criminal fit for stoning; in the modern imagination he is Gandalf, Dumbledore, the wise and kindly master of a benevolent magic. The fantasy is not itself the sin, but it has anaesthetised the conscience: a generation that adores fictional wizards finds it hard to believe the real thing is condemned, and slides easily from the story to the practice. Behind the entertainment stands an actual occult revival — men who style themselves practitioners, mediums, and “chaos magicians,” claiming the very traffic with spirits the law calls a capital crime.

Scripture will not soften. The wizard is bound with the medium under one sentence of death (Lev 20:27), and to consult him is to be defiled (Lev 19:31). Manasseh’s dealing with wizards is named among the sins that filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and brought the nation down. Yet the law that condemns the wizard also displays the LORD who is wiser than every spirit: Isaiah bids the tempted soul turn from the wizards “that peep, and that mutter” (Isa 8:19) to the God who speaks plainly in His word. The believer needs no secret wisdom whispered from the dark; he has Christ, “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” and the fear of the LORD that is wisdom’s beginning.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word is a “wise one” (wys + -ard) — but wise in occult, forbidden things; a male medium.

expand to see more

Wizard — from Middle English wys, “wise,” plus the suffix -ard.

The AV wizard is a man who has occult knowledge through familiar spirits.

He is always paired with the medium and always under the sentence of death (Lev 20:27).

Manasseh dealt with wizards and provoked the LORD to anger (2Ki 21:6).

The modern hero-wizard of fantasy has inverted the word’s meaning entirely.

Usage

"The AV wizard is no kindly Merlin but a man under sentence of stoning (Lev 20:27)."

"A wizard is a “wise one” — wise in the forbidden traffic with familiar spirits."

"Isaiah bids Israel turn from the wizards that peep and mutter to the God who speaks plainly."
